title: Two Women and a Cold Room

pages.text: On Saturdays, Enyonam helped Auntie Comfort sell tomatoes in the market. By afternoon the heat had made the top baskets soft and spotted. Auntie Comfort sorted them with a tight mouth. “Half a basket gone again,” she said, throwing the worst into a bucket. “If I sell cheap, I lose money. If I keep them, they rot.” Enyonam frowned. “There must be a way to keep tomatoes fresh,” she said.

pages.alt: A girl and her aunt sort tomatoes behind market baskets, with spoiled ones in a bucket.

pages.text: At school, Mr Gbeve read from an article from 2018 about a company in Nigeria called ColdHubs. “Its founder says it builds solar-powered cold rooms in markets and on farms,” he said. “Each is run by two women. Traders pay about fifty United States cents per crate for each day of storage. The company says produce lasts up to twenty-one days instead of two. Its figures are reported by the founder, and I have not seen an independent check, so we must be careful.”

“Each is run by two women.
Traders pay about fifty United States cents per crate for each day of storage.
The company says produce lasts up to twenty-one days instead of two.
Its figures are reported by the founder, and I have not seen an independent check, so we must be careful.”
pages.alt: A teacher reads an article beside a drawing of a cold room with solar panels on its roof.

pages.text: “How does it work?” asked Enyonam. “Solar panels collect sunlight and make electricity,” said Mr Gbeve. “The electricity runs a cooling machine, so the room stays cold even when there is no mains power. Cold slows the changes that make vegetables soft and rotten. The article says that in two years, five hubs saved nearly five thousand eight hundred tons of produce and that more than three hundred traders, wholesalers and farmers nearly doubled their monthly income. Again, that is the founder’s report.”

pages.alt: A teacher draws a roof of solar panels, a cooling machine and crates of vegetables in a cold room.

pages.text: The class made a list of honest questions. Would the idea work at their market? How much would solar panels and a cold room cost? Who would own it, and who would pay for repairs? Would traders trust it? Would it be safe and clean? “Good questions,” said Mr Gbeve. “A good idea in one country must be tested before it is copied. And a cold room is only one part. Roads, packaging and buyers also matter.”

pages.text: “It also creates work,” said Mr Gbeve. “According to the article, two women run each hub, and the traders pay for what they use, a crate at a time. That means a market woman does not need to buy a cold room. She needs only to pay for the space she uses.” Enyonam wrote: shared cost, shared benefit. “A cooperative or the market association could think about the same idea,” she said. “If it makes financial sense.”

pages.text: Enyonam did a sum. “Suppose Auntie Comfort stores twenty crates for one day,” she wrote. “If the price were fifty cents a crate, that would be ten dollars. But I must change that into cedis and check whether the saved tomatoes are worth more than the fee.” She stopped. “Suppose she saves two crates that would have rotted. If each is worth eighty cedis, that is one hundred and sixty cedis.” She wrote: all numbers imaginary, so I must find real prices first.

pages.text: The market association invited Enyonam to speak at its monthly meeting. She stood and began: “Mr Chairman, executive members, traders, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon. Today I speak on keeping our food fresh. Every week, many of us throw away tomatoes that the heat has spoiled. Reports from another country show that shared solar cold rooms may help traders keep produce longer. We do not yet know whether this would work here. Therefore, I appeal to this association to study the idea, ask for quotations, and visit an existing cold room. Thank you for listening.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a speech opens with a greeting to the audience, states the topic, gives two or three clear points, makes an appeal or recommendation, and ends with “Thank you”. Enyonam said what she did not know, as well as what she did. Use a polite, spoken tone, no slang and no invented facts. Reading aloud before an exam helps. The end.
